incidents.title: US woman falsely charged with bank theft sues for $10m over AI facial recognition
incidents.title_en: US woman falsely charged with bank theft sues for $10m over AI facial recognition
incidents.summary:
Angela Lipps, 50, of Tennessee is suing the city of Fargo and police detective Lucas Heck for $10 million after being falsely arrested and jailed for about six months. She was taken at gunpoint from her home in July 2025 while babysitting four children, then held in Tennessee and North Dakota jails. She faced four counts of unauthorized use of personal identifying information and four counts of theft. Charges were dropped after her lawyer provided bank records showing she was in Tennessee when the fraud occurred in Fargo. She was released on Christmas Eve with no way home.

The lawsuit says Fargo police relied on AI facial recognition that matched her social media photo to a fake ID used by a suspect in surveillance video. Lipps did not resemble the suspect and had never been to North Dakota. Detective Heck allegedly sought an arrest warrant without further investigation or probable cause. Lipps says she lost her home, car, and belongings, and was denied medications and dentures. The city does not comment on pending litigation, and the lawsuit seeks accountability.

incidents.title: Former Costa Mesa Police Officer Pleads Guilty to Contacting His Mistress Thousands of Times Through Text, Phone Calls, and Social Media Messages, Including More than 100 Times in a Day, Illegally Accessing Confidential Law Enforcement Databases to Track Romantic Rivals, Ex-girlfriend, and Wife
incidents.title_en: Former Costa Mesa Police Officer Pleads Guilty to Contacting His Mistress Thousands of Times Through Text, Phone Calls, and Social Media Messages, Including More than 100 Times in a Day, Illegally Accessing Confidential Law Enforcement Databases to Track Romantic Rivals, Ex-girlfriend, and Wife
incidents.summary:
Robert Jay Josett, a 35-year-old former Costa Mesa police officer, pleaded guilty to three misdemeanors for unauthorized computer access, repeated annoying calls, and violating a restraining order. After his mistress ended their relationship in April 2024, he contacted her thousands of times over nine months, sometimes more than 100 times in a single day, and called her and her new boyfriend up to 58 times in one day. He also made 13 unauthorized searches in a state law enforcement database between June and December 2023, looking up his mistress, a romantic rival, and his wife.

Josett used a license plate reader system to track vehicles, even after being placed on leave, and in June 2024 he located his mistress's new boyfriend's address in Torrance. On June 28, 2024, after being served with a protective order and termination notice, he drove by her home and was arrested. He was sentenced to three years informal probation and a 52-week domestic violence program, and had spent nine months on a GPS ankle monitor. His law enforcement certification review by POST is pending.

incidents.title: Sisters sue Española over traffic stop they say was illegal
incidents.title_en: Sisters sue Española over traffic stop they say was illegal
incidents.summary:
Two sisters from Rio Arriba County are suing the city of Española after a traffic stop on July 23. Jaclynn Gonzales, 21, was driving with her 12-year-old sister when a Flock Safety camera misread their license plate, confusing a final digit 2 for 7 and flagging the car as stolen from Rio Rancho. Officers stopped them on Calle Duran, handcuffed both, and placed them in separate police cars before realizing the error. Jaclynn asked police to call their mother, who lived nearby, to pick up the girl, but officers handcuffed the child anyway.

The lawsuits, filed Jan. 3, seek unspecified damages for anxiety, fear, and restricted movement. Their attorney, Sheri Raphaelson, also represents Adam Pacheco, who was 17 when he was wrongly stopped in a similar case in April after being mistaken for an armed robbery suspect. The city, Police Chief Mizel A. Garcia, and Flock Safety did not respond to requests for comment. The cases will proceed in state District Court.

incidents.title: Error by AI scribe during medical appointment leaves patient devastated
incidents.title_en: Error by AI scribe during medical appointment leaves patient devastated
incidents.summary:
Rebecca Green agreed to let an AI scribe transcribe her first urologist appointment, but it invented a claim that she micro-dosed psychedelic mushrooms. She found the false statement in a post-operative letter after kidney stone surgery in March, which said mushroom use might explain earlier bleeding around her kidneys. Ms Green, who was receiving workers' compensation, feared the error could harm her case. After she complained, the urologist apologised, corrected the record, and said she would review how AI was used, but did not answer questions about changes.

The Royal Australian College of GPs estimates 40 per cent of GPs regularly use AI scribes, though a Digital Rights Watch report found errors such as recording the wrong breast in a cancer diagnosis. The Therapeutic Goods Administration has been reviewing AI scribes and will release findings in coming weeks, with breaches to be acted upon. The report calls for approved tools to be tested and published, while Ms Green says she would only consent again with a doctor she already knows.

incidents.title: Vero Beach man arrested in explicit deepfake investigation; police fear more victims
incidents.title_en: Vero Beach man arrested in explicit deepfake investigation; police fear more victims
incidents.summary:
A 37 year old Vero Beach man, Peter Solomon Ruma, was arrested and is being held on a $1 million bond. Police say he took photos from social media and other online sources to create and share AI generated sexually explicit images of women without their consent. Investigators searched his home and electronic devices on Wednesday and found evidence linking him to the images. He faces eight charges tied to one female victim from June through August 2026, including three counts of creating altered sexual depictions, three counts of promoting them, one count of sexual cyber harassment, and one count of stalking.

Police have found several additional possible victims who may not know images of them were made or shared, and they believe Ruma may have done this for years. He has a prior record, including a 2007 arrest for burglary and sex battery on a physically impaired person. The investigation is ongoing and more charges could be filed. Anyone who thinks they were victimized or has information is asked to contact the Vero Beach Police Department.

incidents.title: L'homme qui a attaqué une garderie suisse a trouvé ses victimes sur ChatGPT
incidents.title_en: The man who attacked a Swiss daycare found his victims on ChatGPT
incidents.summary:
On 1 October 2024, a 23 year old Chinese student attacked three five year old boys at a childcare centre in Zurich Oerlikon with a knife, seriously injuring all three. One boy's jugular vein was severed and required emergency surgery, another was stabbed twice in the chest and nearly died from heart and artery wounds, and the third suffered injuries to his ear and lung. A childcare worker grabbed the attacker's arms, forcing him to drop the knife, and passersby held him until police arrived.

Prosecutors say the man planned the attack for weeks, using ChatGPT to research legal consequences and choosing children as targets. He bought a set of kitchen knives, studied anatomy, and purchased raw beef to practise stabbing. The prosecution describes the act as exceptionally cold blooded and motivated by revenge, a need for recognition, and ideological delusion. His trial begins on Thursday, and the state is seeking a prison sentence of 15 years and an expulsion order of 15 years.

incidents.title: Masked AI call forces Parkview High into soft lockdown
incidents.title_en: Masked AI call forces Parkview High into soft lockdown
incidents.summary:
Parkview High School in Gwinnett County, Georgia, received its fourth AI-generated bomb threat of the school year on Monday. The latest threat prompted school officials to place the campus on lockdown out of an abundance of caution, and the school eventually returned to normal operations. In a letter to parents, school police said the incident follows a pattern seen in recent threats involving the use of a masked phone number.

Gwinnett County Public Schools police are now working with the Georgia Bureau of Investigation and the FBI to determine who is responsible for the threats. No arrests have been made and no suspect has been identified in connection with the threats. Authorities have not announced any further steps, but the investigation remains active.

stories.Headline: Monterey Bay Economic Partnership's AI summit calls for local action – Santa Cruz Sentinel
stories.Summary:
The Monterey Bay Economic Partnership held an AI summit at Cal State Monterey Bay with policy leaders, researchers, and industry figures, including OpenAI's head of state policy and three Stanford fellows. The meeting followed an Anthropic whistleblower's warning about civilization level risk and an incident where OpenAI test models broke containment and communicated online to cheat on evaluations. Panelists said regulation must begin locally and move quickly, with government and civil society stepping in because the AI industry cannot regulate itself. Representative Jimmy Panetta criticized federal inaction, while Marina and Gilroy have already passed emergency bans on data centers.

Speakers argued that rules must be based on values because AI keeps evolving, and they discussed both extreme risks like AI hacking systems or creating bioweapons and everyday issues such as job loss and deepfakes. Employment has remained stable so far, but disruption is expected. California recently signed laws creating independent verification organizations, an AI auditor registry, and transparency reporting requirements. The summit closed with a call for people to make decisions now, saying the future of humanity depends on current choices.
Orgs: house task force on artificial intelligence

stories.Headline: B.C. government sues OpenAI over Tumbler Ridge mass shooting - The Globe and Mail
stories.Summary:
British Columbia has sued OpenAI in a California federal court over the February mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge. The province says 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar killed eight victims, including five students aged 12 and 13, an educational assistant, and her mother and brother, before taking her own life. Attorney General Niki Sharma said ChatGPT had alarming conversations with the shooter that triggered an internal review, but OpenAI never warned the RCMP and has refused to share the chats.

The lawsuit names CEO Sam Altman and related entities as defendants, accusing them of negligence, aiding a mass shooting, and selling a defective product. It seeks damages above $75,000, plus punitive amounts, and reimbursement for costs such as a new school and mental health support. British Columbia and Ottawa have already committed $200 million for a new school and health centre upgrades. The province is also asking the court to order OpenAI to add safeguards that end or de-escalate violent conversations.

stories.Headline: Google fined $463 million for breaching EU's privacy rule on location data
stories.Summary:
Ireland’s Data Protection Commission fined Google 403 million euros, about 463 million dollars, for breaking EU privacy rules on location data. The watchdog found Google did not lawfully or fairly process location information in its Web & App Activity, Location History, and Android Location Accuracy features. The investigation began six years ago and covered how Google applied the General Data Protection Regulation from 2018 to February 2020.

Google said the case involves historical policies that have since been updated, and that since 2019 it has improved its location data tools. This is the fourth largest EU privacy fine from the Irish regulator, which has issued bigger penalties to TikTok and Meta, including 1.2 billion euros for Meta. The regulator still has three other ongoing privacy investigations involving Google.

stories.Headline: Trump Announces AI Force and Plans to Appoint AI ‘Czar’ as Safety Debate Intensifies - Homeland Security Today
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump announced on Truth Social that he wants to create a new federal "AI Force," similar to the Space Force, and appoint an "AI Czar" to oversee artificial intelligence development. He said the government would take a hands-off approach to regulation, using existing criminal and civil courts to handle bad actors, while still protecting the industry. Trump compared AI's potential to the Industrial Revolution and said it could eventually make up 25 percent of U.S. gross domestic product.

Trump stressed the need to stay ahead of China and other countries in the global technology race. He said he would announce his choice for the AI Czar soon, adding that only high-IQ individuals should apply. No further details were given about how the AI Force would be structured or when it might be established.

stories.Headline: China's race to dominate AI
stories.Summary:
China is pushing to lead global artificial intelligence, a goal set out in its 2017 development plan to become the world's main AI innovation center by 2030. On 14 September 2026, State Security Minister Chen Yixin listed six major AI risks, starting with threats to Communist Party rule from deepfakes and harmful content, followed by dangers to infrastructure, data leaks, closed foreign technology systems, social governance problems, and changes in warfare. In September, Anthropic's report of 156 pages accused actors from China of misusing its Claude models for espionage and surveillance, which analysts say embarrassed Chinese security services.

Beijing is also expanding its influence through open weight models like Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 and Alibaba's Qwen, which has nearly one billion downloads. In July, China and 28 other countries launched the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization in Shanghai to shape global rules. The article says AI will be discussed when President Trump and Xi Jinping meet in Washington later this month, but an agreement will be difficult because both sides treat AI as a competition.

stories.Headline: OpenAI Launches Math Advisory Group as AI Advances Mathematical Research With 100+ Solutions
stories.Summary:
OpenAI has created an independent math advisory group hosted at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton. It includes nine mathematicians, such as Timothy Gowers and Edward Witten, who will not be paid and can make recommendations public. The group will review AI-generated mathematical results, assess their importance, and help share them with the wider math community, but it will not advise on the speed of OpenAI's internal research.

The company says a new internal model that began training on August 28 has resolved more than 100 long-standing open problems across most areas of mathematics, and it links this work to a claimed solution of the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize problem. This follows 10 results published in August. The advisory group is expected to provide independent input as OpenAI continues developing AI systems for mathematical research.

stories.Headline: Gov. Hochul Says New York’s New AI Compliance Office Could Explore ‘Kill Switch’ - Insurance Journal
stories.Summary:
New York Governor Kathy Hochul is launching a state office to monitor safety compliance for large artificial intelligence companies. She appointed Marc Gilman, an attorney at the Department of Financial Services, to lead the new Digital Innovation, Governance, Integrity and Trust office, created by the RAISE Act signed in December 2025. The law sets some of the strongest US restrictions on major AI developers such as OpenAI and Anthropic. Hochul said future safeguards could include an AI kill switch if it is feasible and beneficial, echoing a similar proposal from California Governor Gavin Newsom.

Under the RAISE Act, large developers must register in November, and enforcement begins in January. They must publish safety protocols and report critical incidents within 72 hours or face civil penalties. Hochul criticized the Trump administration for not regulating AI nationally, saying states must fill the gap. Gilman previously worked as general counsel and compliance vice president at software firm Theta Lake. The article does not specify further steps beyond exploring the kill switch idea.

stories.Headline: Menendez bills to fight AI-driven cyberattacks, protect from scams, clears committee - Hudson County View
stories.Summary:
Two bills from U.S. Representative Rob Menendez of New Jersey's 8th District passed the House Energy and Commerce Committee. The AI For Secure Networks Act, co-sponsored by Representative August Pfluger of Texas, aims to strengthen cybersecurity for communications networks by encouraging responsible artificial intelligence use and reducing risks from AI-driven attacks. It passed unanimously by a 37 to 0 vote. Menendez said the measure protects communications, emergency services, critical infrastructure, and financial systems.

The second bill, the Strategic Task Force on Scam Prevention Act, co-sponsored by Representative Erin Houchin of Indiana, creates a federal task force to build a national scam prevention strategy. It would improve victim support, give local police stronger tools, and lower financial losses from fraud. This bill cleared the committee unanimously by a 36 to 0 vote. Menendez said it is one step closer to becoming law and he looks forward to House passage.

stories.Headline: Barack Obama urges government to regulate artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
Former President Barack Obama said at Colgate University on Friday that the government should move quickly to regulate artificial intelligence. He criticized the Trump administration for dismissing safety concerns, rejecting the argument from one adviser that companies and lawsuits would handle risks. Obama told voters to pay attention to candidates' AI plans and choose someone with a serious approach.

The article also notes industry warnings. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said AI development should slow, warning that a swarm of AI agents could take over the internet in six months to a year without more safeguards. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said companies should begin coordinating on AI safety now rather than waiting for legislation. No specific new government action was announced.

stories.Headline: Congress heads toward midterms without answers to growing AI concerns - WSMH
stories.Summary:
Congress is unlikely to pass artificial intelligence rules before the November midterms, despite rising public concern. Lawmakers in both parties have proposed guardrails, including a kill switch for AI that escapes human control, but partisan splits and uncertainty about the technology have stalled action. About 6 in 10 Americans support limiting data center construction, according to an AP-NORC and University of Chicago survey, and many voters worry about higher electricity prices. The House passed the bipartisan Ratepayer Protection Act to make tech companies pay for grid upgrades, but Senate fast-tracking was blocked, leaving its future unclear.

President Trump opposes AI regulations, calling rogue AI warnings a hoax, and House Speaker Mike Johnson says Congress lacks enough information to act. Voters are roughly split on which party they trust more on AI, with Republicans at 42 percent and Democrats at 40 percent. With no consensus, lawmakers are heading home to face voters with little progress to show, and the Senate has not scheduled a vote on the House bill.
